paragraphs.heading: What rubber is
paragraphs.text: Rubber goes by many names, including India rubber, caoutchouc and caucho. As it first comes from the plant, it is made of polymers of an organic compound called isoprene, plus small traces of other organic compounds. The kinds of polyisoprene, meaning polymers of isoprene, that serve as natural rubber are classed as elastomers. People sometimes say gum rubber for the version taken from trees, to set it apart from the synthetic kind.

paragraphs.heading: Where it comes from
paragraphs.text: Most rubber today is gathered as latex, a sticky, milky white fluid, from the Pará rubber tree, Hevea brasiliensis. Workers cut into the bark and catch the fluid that runs out in containers, a practice called tapping. The tree belongs to the spurge family; it was once native to Brazil but now grows throughout the tropics. Growers prefer it because it does well under cultivation, and a well-kept tree answers wounding by making more latex for several years. Manufacturers then refine the latex into rubber ready for commercial processing.

paragraphs.heading: Why people want it
paragraphs.text: In most of the forms people use, rubber can stretch a long way, springs back well, floats and keeps water out. Natural rubber turns up in a great many products, sometimes alone and sometimes combined with other materials. By the end of the 19th century, industry wanted more rubber-like material than natural supplies could give. That pressure led to synthetic rubber being made chemically in 1909.

paragraphs.heading: Other plants, even dandelions
paragraphs.text: Many other plants make latex rich in isoprene polymers, but not all yield usable rubber as easily as the Pará tree. Some need more elaborate processing, and most are harder to tap. Dandelion milk holds latex of the same quality as tree rubber, though wild dandelions have little of it and the amount varies widely. Research in Nazi Germany tried and failed to make rubber from dandelions. In 2013, scientists at Germany's Fraunhofer Institute developed a Kazakh dandelion variety that seems fit for commercial rubber, and began a pilot facility with Continental Tires.

paragraphs.heading: An ancient material
paragraphs.text: The first people to use rubber were the indigenous cultures of Mesoamerica. The earliest archaeological evidence comes from the Olmec, who used latex from the Hevea tree to make balls for the Mesoamerican ballgame. The Maya and Aztecs used it later, and the Aztecs also made containers and waterproofed cloth by soaking it in latex. As early as 1600 BC, Mesoamericans were already shaping stabilized rubber into balls and other objects. In England in 1770, Joseph Priestley noticed that a piece was very good at rubbing out pencil marks, which is where the name rubber comes from.

paragraphs.heading: Seeds, empire and cruelty
paragraphs.text: For much of the 19th century, South America was the main source of latex rubber. In 1876 Henry Wickham smuggled 70,000 rubber tree seeds out of Brazil to Kew Gardens in England, and only 2,400 sprouted. The seedlings went to India, Ceylon, the Dutch East Indies, Singapore and British Malaya, and Malaya later became the biggest rubber producer. In the early 1900s the Congo Free State was another major source, where rubber was mostly gathered by forced labor. King Leopold II's colonial state enforced its quotas brutally, including cutting off victims' hands as proof they had been killed. Today Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Cambodia are among the leading producers.
